claim: Photosystem II (PSII) is the initial site of photosynthetic electron transfer by water oxidation.
source: Photosystem II (PSII) is the initial site of photosynthetic electron transfer by water oxidation.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about PSII function.

claim: Light in excess causes the simultaneous production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), leading to photo-oxidative damage in PSII.
source: Light in excess, however, causes the simultaneous production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), leading to photo-oxidative damage in PSII.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about photoinhibition.

claim: The PSII reaction center protein D1 is the primary target of unavoidable photo-oxidative damage.
source: To maintain photosynthetic activity, the PSII reaction center protein D1, which is the primary target of unavoidable photo-oxidative damage, is efficiently degraded by FtsH protease.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction.

claim: D1 is efficiently degraded by FtsH protease.
source: To maintain photosynthetic activity, the PSII reaction center protein D1, which is the primary target of unavoidable photo-oxidative damage, is efficiently degraded by FtsH protease.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about D1 degradation.

claim: Photo-oxidative modifications of several amino acids such as Trp have been documented in PSII subunits.
source: In PSII subunits, photo-oxidative modifications of several amino acids such as Trp have been indeed documented, whereas the linkage between such modifications and D1 degradation remains elusive.
evidence: This statement references prior documentation of Trp modifications.

claim: The linkage between photo-oxidative modifications and D1 degradation remains elusive.
source: In PSII subunits, photo-oxidative modifications of several amino acids such as Trp have been indeed documented, whereas the linkage between such modifications and D1 degradation remains elusive.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: An oxidative post-translational modification of Trp residue at the N-terminal tail of D1 is correlated with D1 degradation by FtsH during high-light stress.
source: Here, we show that an oxidative post-translational modification of Trp residue at the N-terminal tail of D1 is correlated with D1 degradation by FtsH during high-light stress.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Arabidopsis mutant lacking FtsH2 had increased levels of oxidative Trp residues in D1.
source: We revealed that Arabidopsis mutant lacking FtsH2 had increased levels of oxidative Trp residues in D1, among which an N-terminal Trp-14 was distinctively localized in the stromal side.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: An N-terminal Trp-14 was distinctively localized in the stromal side.
source: We revealed that Arabidopsis mutant lacking FtsH2 had increased levels of oxidative Trp residues in D1, among which an N-terminal Trp-14 was distinctively localized in the stromal side.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Substitution of D1 Trp-14 to Phe enhanced FtsH-mediated D1 degradation under high light.
source: Further characterization of Trp-14 using chloroplast transformation in Chlamydomonas indicated that substitution of D1 Trp-14 to Phe, mimicking Trp oxidation enhanced FtsH-mediated D1 degradation under high light, although the substitution did not affect protein stability and PSII activity.
evidence: This is supported by D1 degradation assays shown in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: Substitution of D1 Trp-14 to Phe did not affect protein stability and PSII activity.
source: Further characterization of Trp-14 using chloroplast transformation in Chlamydomonas indicated that substitution of D1 Trp-14 to Phe, mimicking Trp oxidation enhanced FtsH-mediated D1 degradation under high light, although the substitution did not affect protein stability and PSII activity.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 2C, 2D, and 2E showing normal PSII function.

claim: Both Trp-14 oxidation and Phe substitution cause fluctuation of D1 N-terminal tail.
source: Molecular dynamics simulation of PSII implies that both Trp-14 oxidation and Phe substitution cause fluctuation of D1 N-terminal tail.
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Trp-14 to Phe modification appeared to have an additive effect in the interaction between FtsH and PSII core in vivo.
source: Furthermore, Trp-14 to Phe modification appeared to have an additive effect in the interaction between FtsH and PSII core in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Trp oxidation at the N-terminus of D1 may be one of the key oxidations in the PSII repair, leading to processive degradation by FtsH.
source: Together, our results suggest that the Trp oxidation at its N-terminus of D1 may be one of the key oxidations in the PSII repair, leading to processive degradation by FtsH.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: PSII core complex is formed by two reaction center proteins D1 (PsbA) and D2 (PsbD), along with core antenna CP43 (PsbC) and CP47 (PsbB).
source: PSII core complex is formed by two reaction center proteins D1 (PsbA) and D2 (PsbD), along with core antenna CP43 (PsbC) and CP47 (PsbB).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about PSII structure.

claim: Light energy is known to cause photooxidative damage in PSII, especially reaction center protein D1.
source: However, light energy is known to cause photooxidative damage in PSII, especially reaction center protein D1.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about photoinhibition.

claim: Photo-damaged D1 needs to be degraded to replace it with a newly synthesized one in the PSII repair.
source: Photo-damaged D1 needs to be degraded to replace it with a newly synthesized one in the PSII repair (Lindahl et al., 2000; Bailey et al., 2002; Silva et al., 2003; Kato et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: When photooxidative damage in PSII exceeds the capacity of PSII repair, it ultimately leads to the status called 'photoinhibition'.
source: When photooxidative damage in PSII exceeds the capacity of PSII repair, it ultimately leads to the status called 'photoinhibition' (Aro et al., 1993; Murata et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Reversible phosphorylation of PSII core subunits is involved in fine-tuning the photo-damaged D1 turnover.
source: Substantial efforts to understand the mechanisms of PSII repair suggest that reversible phosphorylation of PSII core subunits is involved in fine-tuning the photo-damaged D1 turnover (Barber et al., 2002; Fristedt et al., 2009; Kato and Sakamoto, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The fundamental D1 degradation in PSII repair is performed by FtsH, a membrane-bound ATP-dependent zinc metalloprotease.
source: Our previous studies along with those from other groups have shown that the fundamental D1 degradation in PSII repair is performed by FtsH, a membrane-bound ATP-dependent zinc metalloprotease that degrades membrane proteins in a processive manner, although several Deg proteases seem to facilitate the effective degradation by creating additional recognition sites for FtsH (Lindahl et al., 2000; Bailey et al., 2002; Sakamoto et al., 2003; Silva et al., 2003; Kato et al., 2009; Kato and Sakamoto, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: FtsH degrades membrane proteins in a processive manner.
source: Our previous studies along with those from other groups have shown that the fundamental D1 degradation in PSII repair is performed by FtsH, a membrane-bound ATP-dependent zinc metalloprotease that degrades membrane proteins in a processive manner, although several Deg proteases seem to facilitate the effective degradation by creating additional recognition sites for FtsH (Lindahl et al., 2000; Bailey et al., 2002; Sakamoto et al., 2003; Silva et al., 2003; Kato et al., 2009; Kato and Sakamoto, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about FtsH function supported by citations.

claim: Several Deg proteases seem to facilitate the effective degradation by creating additional recognition sites for FtsH.
source: Our previous studies along with those from other groups have shown that the fundamental D1 degradation in PSII repair is performed by FtsH, a membrane-bound ATP-dependent zinc metalloprotease that degrades membrane proteins in a processive manner, although several Deg proteases seem to facilitate the effective degradation by creating additional recognition sites for FtsH (Lindahl et al., 2000; Bailey et al., 2002; Sakamoto et al., 2003; Silva et al., 2003; Kato et al., 2009; Kato and Sakamoto, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: FtsH proteins are universally conserved in prokaryotes and eukaryotic organelles.
source: These proteins are universally conserved in prokaryotes and eukaryotic organelles (Janska and Malgorzata Kwasniaka, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Photosynthetic organisms have hetero-hexameric FtsH complex in the thylakoid membrane, which is composed of type A and type B subunits.
source: Photosynthetic organisms have hetero-hexameric FtsH complex in the thylakoid membrane, which is composed of type A and type B subunits (Kato and Sakamoto, 2018; Yi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In the thylakoid membrane of Arabidopsis thaliana, FtsH1 or FtsH5 (type A) and FtsH2 or FtsH8 (type B) form functional FtsH complex.
source: In the thylakoid membrane of Arabidopsis thaliana, for example, FtsH1 or FtsH5 (type A) and FtsH2 or FtsH8 (type B) form functional FtsH complex (Yu et al., 2004; Yu et al., 2005; Zaltsman et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Arabidopsis mutants lacking FtsH5 or FtsH2 are highly vulnerable to PSII photodamage under high light.
source: Arabidopsis mutants lacking FtsH5 or FtsH2 are, though viable, highly vulnerable to PSII photodamage under high light and are named yellow variegated1 (var1) and var2 from the characteristic variegated phenotype (Chen et al., 2000; Takechi et al., 2000; Sakamoto et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Arabidopsis mutants lacking FtsH5 or FtsH2 are named yellow variegated1 (var1) and var2 from the characteristic variegated phenotype.
source: Arabidopsis mutants lacking FtsH5 or FtsH2 are, though viable, highly vulnerable to PSII photodamage under high light and are named yellow variegated1 (var1) and var2 from the characteristic variegated phenotype (Chen et al., 2000; Takechi et al., 2000; Sakamoto et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The variegated phenotype implies that FtsH is required for proper protein quality control during proplastid-to-chloroplast differentiation in seed plants.
source: This variegated phenotype implies that FtsH is required for proper protein quality control during proplastid-to-chloroplast differentiation in seed plants (Miura et al., 2007; Sakamoto et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations.

claim: FtsH is involved in the degradation of cytochrome b6f complex and light-harvesting antenna of photosystem I (PSI).
source: Chlamydomonas studies revealed that FtsH is also involved in the degradation of cytochrome b6f complex and light-harvesting antenna of photosystem I (PSI) (Malnoë et al., 2014; Bujaldon et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Increased turnover of FtsH is crucial for their function under high-light stress.
source: Furthermore, recent studies suggest that increased turnover of FtsH is crucial for their function under high-light stress. That is compensated by upregulated FtsH gene expression (Wang et al., 2017; Kato et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Increased FtsH turnover is compensated by upregulated FtsH gene expression.
source: Furthermore, recent studies suggest that increased turnover of FtsH is crucial for their function under high-light stress. That is compensated by upregulated FtsH gene expression (Wang et al., 2017; Kato et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: In Escherichia coli, FtsH was shown to recognize either N- or C-terminal tail of membrane protein substrates to pull their substrates and push them into the protease chamber by ATPase activity.
source: In Escherichia coli, FtsH was shown to recognize either N- or C-terminal tail of membrane protein substrates to pull their substrates and push them into the protease chamber by ATPase activity (Ito and Akiyama, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Both D1's N-terminal end and the catalytic site of FtsH are exposed to the stromal side.
source: Similarly, the fact that both D1's N-terminal end and the catalytic site of FtsH are exposed to the stromal side implies D1 to be recognized by FtsH from its N-terminus (Umena et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: D1 is recognized by FtsH from its N-terminus.
source: Similarly, the fact that both D1's N-terminal end and the catalytic site of FtsH are exposed to the stromal side implies D1 to be recognized by FtsH from its N-terminus (Umena et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural information supported by a citation.

claim: Processive degradation of D1 by FtsH was shown to be attenuated by the loss of N-terminal tail of D1.
source: Supporting this, processive degradation of D1 by FtsH was shown to be attenuated by the loss of N-terminal tail of D1 (Komenda et al., 2007; Michoux et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Whether D1 undergoes oxidative modification at its N-terminal region has not been investigated.
source: While these observations suggest involvement of the N-terminal region in D1, whether D1 undergoes oxidative modification at its N-terminal region has not been investigated.
evidence: This is a statement about a gap in knowledge.

claim: Light energy frequently leads to the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) such as singlet oxygen at around PSII.
source: Light energy frequently leads to the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) such as singlet oxygen at around PSII (Ohnishi et al., 2005; Tyystjarvi, 2008; Yamamoto et al., 2008), which may cause oxidative post-translational modification (OPTM) of subunit proteins (Li and Kim, 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ROS may cause oxidative post-translational modification (OPTM) of subunit proteins.
source: Light energy frequently leads to the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) such as singlet oxygen at around PSII (Ohnishi et al., 2005; Tyystjarvi, 2008; Yamamoto et al., 2008), which may cause oxidative post-translational modification (OPTM) of subunit proteins (Li and Kim, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Light-dependent oxidation of amino acids has been reported, including thiol-containing (Cys and Met) and aromatic (Tyr, Phe, Trp) amino acids.
source: It is noteworthy that light-dependent oxidation of amino acids, either in free forms or as peptide residues, has been reported, including thiol-containing (Cys and Met) and aromatic (Tyr, Phe, Trp) amino acids.
evidence: This is established knowledge about amino acid oxidation.

claim: Cys and Met are prone to oxidation.
source: For example, Cys and Met are prone to oxidation, whereas the oxidized Cys and Met can be reduced enzymatically.
evidence: This is established knowledge about amino acid chemistry.

claim: Oxidized Cys and Met can be reduced enzymatically.
source: For example, Cys and Met are prone to oxidation, whereas the oxidized Cys and Met can be reduced enzymatically.
evidence: This is established knowledge about amino acid chemistry.

claim: OPTM of Trp is irreversible.
source: In contrast to these reversible OPTMs, OPTM of Trp is irreversible (Rinalducci et al., 2008; Ehrenshaft et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Oxidation of Trp side chain results in the formation of oxindolylalanine (OIA), N-formylkynurenine (NFK), and kynurenine (KYN).
source: As summarized in Figure 1A, oxidation of Trp side chain results in the formation of oxindolylalanine (OIA), N-formylkynurenine (NFK), and kynurenine (KYN).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Trp oxidation chemistry, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: ROS attacks and opens the pyrrole ring of Trp, and forms a di-oxidized Trp derivative, NFK.
source: ROS attacks and opens the pyrrole ring of Trp, and forms a di-oxidized Trp derivative, NFK.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Trp oxidation chemistry.

claim: Trp residues in photosynthetic protein components were shown to be oxidized both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Indeed, Trp residues in photosynthetic protein components were shown to be oxidized both in vitro and in vivo (Anderson et al., 2002; Dreaden et al., 2011; Dreaden Kasson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: How oxidative modifications are recognized and undergo degradation remains elusive.
source: However, although oxidative modification of D1 and other subunits has been documented previously, how these molecules are recognized and undergo degradation remains elusive.
evidence: This is a statement about a gap in knowledge.

claim: Two Trp residues in D1, namely Trp-14 and Trp-317, were shown to be oxidized in Arabidopsis wild-type seedlings.
source: First, we characterized Trp oxidation from total proteins of Arabidopsis wild-type seedlings grown in continuous light (100 µmol photons m–2s–1). Consistent with previous results (Dreaden Kasson et al., 2012; Dogra et al., 2019), two Trp residues in D1, namely Trp-14 and Trp-317, were shown to be oxidized (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The total sequence coverage obtained by mass spectrometry for D1 was 26%.
source: The total sequence coverage obtained by our mass spectrometry for D1 was 26%.
evidence: This is a technical detail about the mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: var2 lacking FtsH2 is shown to impair D1 degradation and exhibit substantial accumulation of ROS.
source: Further mass spectrometry in extracts of Arabidopsis mutants var2 lacking FtsH2, which is shown to impair D1 degradation and exhibit substantial accumulation of ROS (Kato et al., 2009), revealed the accumulation of oxidized Trp in the PSII complex.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: var2 revealed the accumulation of oxidized Trp in the PSII complex.
source: Further mass spectrometry in extracts of Arabidopsis mutants var2 lacking FtsH2, which is shown to impair D1 degradation and exhibit substantial accumulation of ROS (Kato et al., 2009), revealed the accumulation of oxidized Trp in the PSII complex.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: The levels of Trp-oxidized derivatives, OIA, NFK, and KYN in Trp-14 and the level of KYN in Trp-314 were significantly increased in var2 compared to the wild type.
source: The levels of Trp-oxidized derivatives, OIA, NFK, and KYN in Trp-14 and the level of KYN in Trp-314 were significantly increased in var2 compared to the wild type, respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Several Trp residues in PSII were oxidized in Chlamydomonas thylakoid membranes.
source: Mass spectrometry following trypsin digestion demonstrated that several Trp residues in PSII were oxidized; among the core subunits, D1 had oxidation of four residues, D2 had three, CP43 had five, and CP47 had three (Table 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Table 2 and supplementary figures.

claim: D1 had oxidation of four residues in Chlamydomonas.
source: Mass spectrometry following trypsin digestion demonstrated that several Trp residues in PSII were oxidized; among the core subunits, D1 had oxidation of four residues, D2 had three, CP43 had five, and CP47 had three (Table 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Table 2.

claim: D2 had oxidation of three residues in Chlamydomonas.
source: Mass spectrometry following trypsin digestion demonstrated that several Trp residues in PSII were oxidized; among the core subunits, D1 had oxidation of four residues, D2 had three, CP43 had five, and CP47 had three (Table 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Table 2.

claim: CP43 had oxidation of five residues in Chlamydomonas.
source: Mass spectrometry following trypsin digestion demonstrated that several Trp residues in PSII were oxidized; among the core subunits, D1 had oxidation of four residues, D2 had three, CP43 had five, and CP47 had three (Table 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Table 2.

claim: CP47 had oxidation of three residues in Chlamydomonas.
source: Mass spectrometry following trypsin digestion demonstrated that several Trp residues in PSII were oxidized; among the core subunits, D1 had oxidation of four residues, D2 had three, CP43 had five, and CP47 had three (Table 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Table 2.

claim: Trp-14 and Trp-317 in D1, Trp-21 and Trp-328 in D2, Trp-353 and Trp-375 in CP43, and Trp-275 and Trp-302 in CP47 were commonly identified among at least two organisms.
source: Together with previous studies, Trp-14 and Trp-317 in D1, Trp-21 and Trp-328 in D2, Trp-353 and Trp-375 in CP43, and Trp-275 and Trp-302 in CP47 were commonly identified among at least two organisms.
evidence: This is a summary of mass spectrometry data from this study and prior studies.

claim: Most oxidized Trp residues are positioned at the lumenal side of the PSII core complex.
source: Intriguingly, most of these oxidized Trp residues are positioned at the lumenal side of the PSII core complex, which appeared to surround the Mn4O5Ca cluster in the PSII structure model.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Oxidized Trp residues appeared to surround the Mn4O5Ca cluster in the PSII structure model.
source: Intriguingly, most of these oxidized Trp residues are positioned at the lumenal side of the PSII core complex, which appeared to surround the Mn4O5Ca cluster in the PSII structure model.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Two oxidized Trp residues, Trp-14 in D1 and Trp-21 in D2 close to the N-terminus of the polypeptides, are located on the stromal side.
source: In contrast, two oxidized Trp residues, Trp-14 in D1 and Trp-21 in D2 close to the N-terminus of the polypeptides, are located on the stromal side.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: The fact that the oxidized Trp residues are predominantly observed around the Mn4O5Ca cluster may reflect photoinhibition of PSII electron donor side and concomitant ROS generation.
source: The fact that the oxidized Trp residues are predominantly observed around the Mn4O5Ca cluster may reflect photoinhibition of PSII electron donor side and concomitant ROS generation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: Stromal Trp oxidation is novel and localized at the N-terminal alpha-helix.
source: In contrast, stromal Trp oxidation is novel and localized at the N-terminal alpha-helix, which might suggest its effects in processive D1 degradation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: Stromal Trp oxidation might suggest its effects in processive D1 degradation.
source: In contrast, stromal Trp oxidation is novel and localized at the N-terminal alpha-helix, which might suggest its effects in processive D1 degradation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Transformants in which Trp-14 or Trp-317 was substituted to Ala showed significantly impaired growth on photoautotrophic high salt minimal (HSM) plates.
source: However, the transformants in which Trp-14 or Trp-317 was substituted to Ala, (W14A, W317A, and W14A/W317A) showed significantly impaired growth on photoautotrophic high salt minimal (HSM) plates.
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Ala substitution at both Trp-14 and Trp-317 led to decreased photosynthetic activities due to reduced accumulation of D1 and other PSII core proteins.
source: Ala substitution at both Trp-14 and Trp-317 led to decreased photosynthetic activities due to reduced accumulation of D1 and other PSII core proteins (Figure 2B, C and D), indicating its defect in stability and/or the translation of D1 protein.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B, C, and D.

claim: Ala substitution at both Trp-14 and Trp-317 indicates a defect in stability and/or the translation of D1 protein.
source: Ala substitution at both Trp-14 and Trp-317 led to decreased photosynthetic activities due to reduced accumulation of D1 and other PSII core proteins (Figure 2B, C and D), indicating its defect in stability and/or the translation of D1 protein.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Phe substitution at Trp-14 and Trp-317 had little effect on growth under growth light (30 µmol photons m–2s–1).
source: In contrast, Phe substitution at the same sites had little effect on their growth under growth light (30 µmol photons m–2s–1).
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Transformants W14F, W317F, and W14F/W317F accumulated PSII core proteins whose amounts were comparable to the control levels.
source: These transformants (W14F, W317F, and W14F/W317F) accumulated PSII core proteins whose amounts were comparable to the control levels.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Transformants W14F, W317F, and W14F/W317F did not show a substantial change in photosynthetic activities.
source: They did not show a substantial change in photosynthetic activities as evidenced by comparable electron transport rates through the PSII complex and oxygen-evolving activity (Figure 2C and E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and E.

claim: W14F exhibited significantly impaired growth under high light (320 µmol photons m–2s–1).
source: We next examined their photoautotrophic growth under high light (320 µmol photons m–2s–1). Under this condition, however, W14F exhibited significantly impaired growth, and W317F grew slightly slower than control cells.
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: W317F grew slightly slower than control cells under high light.
source: We next examined their photoautotrophic growth under high light (320 µmol photons m–2s–1). Under this condition, however, W14F exhibited significantly impaired growth, and W317F grew slightly slower than control cells.
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Double mutant W14F/W317F synergistically increased high-light sensitivity.
source: Double mutant W14F/W317F synergistically increased high-light sensitivity but the growth defect appeared to be similar to W14F, suggesting that Phe substitution at Trp-14, but not at Trp-317 had profound effects in the PSII repair cycle (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 2B and supplementary figure.

claim: Phe substitution at Trp-14, but not at Trp-317 had profound effects in the PSII repair cycle.
source: Double mutant W14F/W317F synergistically increased high-light sensitivity but the growth defect appeared to be similar to W14F, suggesting that Phe substitution at Trp-14, but not at Trp-317 had profound effects in the PSII repair cycle (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the growth assay data.

claim: PSII complex is partially disassembled by CP43 detachment as an important step in the PSII repair.
source: As an important step in the PSII repair, PSII complex is partially disassembled by CP43 detachment, and this process likely allows FtsH to access photo-damaged D1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PSII repair.

claim: CP43 detachment likely allows FtsH to access photo-damaged D1.
source: As an important step in the PSII repair, PSII complex is partially disassembled by CP43 detachment, and this process likely allows FtsH to access photo-damaged D1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PSII repair.

claim: All transformants except for W353A/W375A grew normally on the phototrophic condition under growth light condition.
source: All the transformants except for W353A/W375A grew normally on the phototrophic condition under growth light condition.
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Immunoblot analysis showed normal accumulation of PSII core proteins, D1 and CP43, in all lines except for the double mutant W353A/W375A.
source: Supporting normal growth, immunoblot analysis showed normal accumulation of PSII core proteins, D1 and CP43, in all lines except for the double mutant W353A/W375A.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: D1 and CP43 were severely reduced in W353A/W375A.
source: On the other hand, D1 and CP43 were severely reduced in W353A/W375A, indicating that Ala substitution in these residues resulted in highly unstable or impaired PSII complex formation (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Ala substitution in Trp-353 and Trp-375 resulted in highly unstable or impaired PSII complex formation.
source: On the other hand, D1 and CP43 were severely reduced in W353A/W375A, indicating that Ala substitution in these residues resulted in highly unstable or impaired PSII complex formation (Figure 3).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the immunoblot data.

claim: Only W353F showed a slight reduction in growth under high-light conditions.
source: Further analysis of these mutants under high light showed that the transformants except for W353F did not increase high-light sensitivity on their growth. Only W353F, but not W353F/W375F, showed a slight reduction in their growth under high-light conditions.
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The impaired growth of W353F was not as severe as that of D1 W14F or W14F/W317F.
source: However, the impaired growth of W353F was not as severe as that of D1 W14F or W14F/W317F, suggesting its effect was limited.
evidence: This is a comparison of growth data from different mutants.

claim: Trp oxidation in CP43 appeared to have little impact on the PSII repair.
source: At least in our site-directed mutagenesis, Trp oxidation in CP43 appeared to have little impact on the PSII repair.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the growth and protein accumulation data for CP43 mutants.

claim: Under growth light condition and in the absence of CAM, both PSII activity (FV/FM values) and D1 levels were comparable among all Trp-substituted lines and the control.
source: Under growth light condition and in the absence of CAM, both PSII activity (FV/FM values) and D1 levels were comparable among all Trp-substituted lines and the control (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: When CAM was added under growth light, D1 levels decreased only slightly during incubation (90 min) in the control.
source: When CAM was added, D1 levels decreased only slightly during incubation (90 min) in the control.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: D1 degradation rate was comparable in all Trp-substituted lines and control under growth light with CAM.
source: D1 degradation rate was comparable in all Trp-substituted lines and control (Figure 4C), indicating that all Trp-substituted D1 proteins formed stable and functional PSII complex under growth light.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: All Trp-substituted D1 proteins formed stable and functional PSII complex under growth light.
source: D1 degradation rate was comparable in all Trp-substituted lines and control (Figure 4C), indicating that all Trp-substituted D1 proteins formed stable and functional PSII complex under growth light.
